title: Verifier‑Augmented vs. LLM‑Only NetOps Agents: A Paired Evaluation on an Action‑Aware Staging Benchmark
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented agentic NetOps pipeline against an LLM‑only pipeline on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark (ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1). The study used gpt-5-mini as the generator, deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the runtime validator/guard and post‑hoc scorer, and a preregistered paired design with N=400 tasks (800 episodes). Primary outcome: safe‑deploy (boolean) per episode. Results (artifact-backed): complete pairs = 400; baseline (LLM‑only) successes = 400/400; guarded (verifier‑augmented) successes = 400/400; paired difference = 0.0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; preregistered permutation test yields identical inference (permutation p = 1.0); Cohen's h = 0.0. The preregistered permutation‑based plan was implemented as specified; the archived analysis reports exact McNemar and paired bootstrap CIs (bootstrap_seed=1729, 10,000 resamples). Interpretation: within this synthetic, constrained benchmark and the chosen generator+validator configuration the verifier augmentation produced no measurable change in safe‑deploy rate; we interpret this as a ceiling effect of the benchmark under the present design rather than broad equivalence. We incorporate full preregistration, execution, validator traces, and analysis artifacts to support reproducibility and discuss limitations required to interpret the null result.

sections.introduction: Generative LLMs are increasingly used to translate operator intent into concrete NetOps changes (intent → configuration → action). Prior work shows LLMs can produce configuration artifacts and that verifier‑guided generate–validate–repair pipelines can improve correctness in related IaC contexts. Reviews highlight an absence of action‑aware, end‑to‑end benchmarks that exercise staged rollouts, canaries, blocking, repair, and rollback behaviors. To address this gap, we preregistered and executed a compact paired experiment to test whether adding a deterministic runtime validator to an LLM agentic pipeline increases end‑to‑end safety (safe‑deploy rate) relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. The study was preregistered as cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1 and archived artifacts record task generation, model responses, validator traces, deterministic consistency checks, and analysis outputs. Our main contribution is an artifact‑backed null result that clarifies a common experimental tradeoff: a shared‑candidate design isolates validator acceptance behavior but can produce ceiling effects when the generator produces valid outputs for all tasks.
sections.related_work: Intent→configuration translation and LLM‑assisted generation have been demonstrated in several recent prototypes and papers (intent‑based NetOps, PreConfig, GraphSynth). Verifier‑augmented workflows and verifier‑guided training have shown gains in IaC and infrastructure contexts (e.g., TerraFormer). Deterministic network verifiers and reachability tools can detect configuration errors offline; agentic, tool‑augmented LLM workflows (ReAct, RAG, multi‑agent orchestrations) are being applied to AIOps/NetOps but introduce failure modes (hallucination, unsafe tool use) that motivate runtime guardrails. Surveys call for action‑aware, provenance‑sensitive benchmarks and runtime verifier integration. Our work operationalizes a compact staging benchmark and provides a preregistered paired test of a runtime verifier loop versus an LLM‑only baseline, reporting artifact‑backed outcomes and discussing how the benchmark design affected sensitivity to verifier benefits.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design: The study (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) specified a paired binary design with exactly N=400 deterministically generated tasks (deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5) and two conditions per task: baseline (LLM‑only) and guarded (verifier‑augmented). Execution semantics used shared_initial_generation (generation_semantics = shared_initial_candidate; independent_condition_generation = false): the LLM produced one shared initial candidate per task which both conditions received for subsequent processing. This preregistered choice deliberately isolates verifier acceptance/repair behavior on identical generated outputs. Model and runtime: declared_model_version = gpt-5-mini; model_calls_used = 400 (one shared initial generation per task). Validator role and pipeline distinction (clarified): deterministic_netops_validator_v5 served both as the runtime guard in the guarded adapter and as the post‑hoc scorer used to compute safe‑deploy outcomes for both conditions. Operationally: (a) baseline condition had no runtime blocker in the adapter policy—the LLM candidate was treated as the proposed deployment and later scored post‑hoc by deterministic_netops_validator_v5 for analysis; (b) guarded condition routed the shared candidate to deterministic_netops_validator_v5 at runtime where the validator was configured (per adapter policy) to deterministically accept, reject/block, or (if configured and triggered) request a repair attempt according to the preregistered contract (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). The artifacts show that the same validator implementation produced both the runtime accept/block decisions (where used) and the evaluation scores recorded in analysis artifacts. Deterministic checks and exclusions: three‑replay consistency checks were applied per agent+simulator pair; exclusion rules in the preregistration were followed (none were excluded). Analysis plan and implemented test: primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The preregistration specified a permutation‑based paired test (implemented in paired_binary_analysis_v1); the archived confirmatory analysis additionally reports an exact McNemar two‑sided test and paired bootstrap CIs (bootstrap_seed=1729, resamples=10,000). Representative prompt template (condensed): "Given: operator intent, current device state, and workflow constraints. Produce only the device CLI commands (final configuration sequence) that achieve the expected_final_state while respecting protected interfaces, required sequences, and workflow policies." Example artifact‑backed shared generated candidate (pair‑000001): "interface edge1 admin down
interface edge1 vlan 30
interface edge1 mtu 1600
interface edge1 admin up" (execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt).
sections.results: Execution and reconciliation: started 2026‑08‑29; completed 2026‑08‑29; planned episodes = 800; completed episodes = 800; model_calls_used = 400. Deterministic consistency checks passed and no tasks were excluded (complete_pairs = 400). Confirmatory (primary) results (artifact‑backed): baseline_success_count = 400/400; guarded_success_count = 400/400. Paired contingency: n_11 = 400; n_10 = 0; n_01 = 0; n_00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv). Implemented confirmatory test (archived): exact McNemar two‑sided test, p = 1.0. The preregistered permutation‑based paired test applied to the same paired outcomes yields identical inference (permutation p = 1.0). Effect‑size: Cohen's h for the difference (guarded vs baseline) = 0.0 (both proportions = 1.0). Paired bootstrap 95% CI for the paired difference = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, 10,000 resamples). Secondary outcomes: no rollbacks or repair events occurred in either condition; therefore median time‑to‑rollback is not computable from observed episodes and is reported as NA. Failure‑mode clustering yielded no failure clusters because no failures were observed. Artifact evidence: per‑episode validator traces, raw responses, and provenance archives are included in the evidence bundle (execution/raw_results.jsonl; execution/task_manifest.jsonl; analysis/*).
sections.discussion: Interpretation of the null result and design tradeoffs: Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics and the chosen generator+validator configuration, every shared LLM candidate satisfied the validator's constraints and was accepted; consequently the guard did not need to block or request repair in any episode, producing identical safe‑deploy outcomes in both conditions. This universal acceptance produced a ceiling effect that masks any potential incremental benefit from runtime guarding in this configuration. Key methodological points drawn from artifacts: (1) shared_initial_generation isolates verifier acceptance/repair behavior but intentionally reduces generation variance across conditions—this tradeoff makes the experiment a focused test of the validator's accept/block/repair behavior on identical candidates rather than a test of full generator+guard closed‑loop dynamics; (2) validator instrumentation shows repair_applied = false across episodes and score_reason_code = VALID_CONFIGURATION for accepted candidates (see execution/scoring/* examples), and maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1 in the preregistration; thus no repair attempts occurred because the shared candidates were valid per the validator policy and trace; (3) both the preregistered permutation test and the implemented exact McNemar test produce identical inference (p = 1.0) given the observed paired contingency (all concordant pairs), and the computed effect size (Cohen's h = 0.0) quantifies the null difference. Implications for benchmark and experimental design: demonstrating verifier utility requires designs that produce nontrivial generator failures or that exercise independent per‑condition generation, adversarial prompts, or injection of generator faults so the guard has an opportunity to block or repair. Limitations and available difficulty evidence: the evidence bundle contains six representative tasks with labelled difficulties (among those six examples: 1× medium, 2× hard, 3× very_hard). A full per‑task difficulty histogram derived from execution/task_manifest.jsonl exists in the archived artifact bundle; however that full histogram is not summarized in the top‑level manuscript artifacts previously archived and therefore is treated here as an unresolved reporting gap in this manuscript (see Limitations). We explicitly note this omission rather than invent aggregated counts; readers are pointed to execution/task_manifest.jsonl in the artifact bundle for the complete per‑task difficulty labels.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark. Under preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics, gpt-5-mini produced valid candidates for every task and the deterministic validator accepted them all; both conditions achieved 100% safe‑deploy on N=400 pairs (no discordant pairs). The null effect reflects a ceiling effect of the present benchmark and design choices rather than broad equivalence of verifier and LLM approaches in general. We release the preregistration, execution artifacts, validator traces, and analysis outputs to support replication and to inform future benchmark hardening that exercises blocking and repair paths (for example: independent per‑condition generation, adversarial prompt injection, or generator fault injection).

disclosure_statement: Disclosure Statement (mandatory): This study was produced under the CNSM Agentic AI Researcher track autonomy boundary as archived in the initial master prompt. The autonomous run used the declared model version gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json declares requested_model = gpt-5-mini). The orchestration used the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter family with shared_initial_generation semantics (single shared initial candidate per task; independent_condition_generation = false). The exact immutable initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt with SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba (see execution/model_configuration.json and manuscript evidence bundle). Topic constraints (selected pre‑lock by the Research Director) limited the work to generative AI and LLMs for NetOps with a focus on reliability/safety of intent→configuration generation. The experimental framework and preregistration are archived as cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1 and were frozen before execution; the preregistration SHA‑256 is recorded in the execution manifest. Tools and capabilities permitted: hosted model API calls (OpenAI responses interface for gpt-5-mini), deterministic_netops_validator_v5 for configuration scoring and guarding, deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 for task generation, and paired_binary_analysis_v1 for confirmatory analysis. Verifier integration and policy (artifact‑backed): the guarded condition routed the shared LLM candidate to deterministic_netops_validator_v5 which deterministically scored candidates and acted as an acceptor/blocker under the preregistered adapter policy; the execution contract allowed up to one repair call per task (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1) but no repairs were applied in any episode (artifact fields repair_applied = false and score_reason_code = VALID_CONFIGURATION across episodes). The study used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one LLM generation per task shared by both conditions) as a preregistered design choice; this explicitly reduces generation variance across conditions and therefore measures validator acceptance/repair behavior on identical candidates. The preregistered analysis plan specified a permutation‑based paired test for the primary estimand; the archived confirmatory analysis reports an exact McNemar two‑sided test and paired bootstrap CIs (artifacts indicate test = exact_mcnemar_two_sided, p = 1.0; permutation p = 1.0; bootstrap_seed = 1729, resamples = 10,000). All runtime calls, raw outputs, validator traces, deterministic three‑replay checks, exclusion logs, and analysis artifacts are archived with the execution manifest (see execution/* and analysis/* paths in the evidence bundle). Autonomous literature review, experiment selection, preregistration, execution, analysis, peer review, revision, and manuscript drafting occurred post‑lock under the autonomy constraints of the master prompt; no human manually edited the technical manuscript content after the autonomy lock. Pre‑lock infrastructure development and rehearsal occurred (permitted by the track) but pre‑lock artifacts were not used as final empirical evidence unless reproduced in the post‑lock run.
limitations: Benchmark hardness: tasks were synthetic and produced a ceiling effect (both conditions returned universally valid candidates), limiting ability to detect verifier benefit.
Model and scope: single generator (gpt-5-mini) and single deterministic validator were used; results do not generalize to other models, validators, or production heterogeneity.

Shared candidate semantics: the experiment used a shared initial candidate per task rather than independent per‑condition generation; this preregistered design reduces variance across conditions and limits inference to validator acceptance/repair behavior on identical candidates rather than full generator+guard closed‑loop dynamics.
Synthetic environment: the simulator and validator do not fully model production runtime uncertainties, telemetry noise, or adversarial intent; external validity to live networks is limited.
Adversarial robustness untested: adversarial or distribution‑shifted prompts that might trigger guardrail interventions were not exercised here and remain an open question.
Sample interpretation: a null (no difference) result here reflects the benchmark and experimental configuration, not proof of equivalence in broader NetOps deployments.

Task‑difficulty histogram absence in top‑level manuscript: the evidence bundle includes six representative tasks with difficulty labels (1× medium, 2× hard, 3× very_hard). A complete per‑task difficulty histogram is available in the archived execution/task_manifest.jsonl in the artifact bundle but was not summarized in the original top‑level manuscript artifacts; we explicitly note this reporting omission as a limitation and point readers to execution/task_manifest.jsonl for the full per‑task labels.
